item.research_question: How does long-term thermal exposure at 1000 °C affect the structural stability, grain growth kinetics, and mechanical properties of a TiCoCrFeMn high-entropy alloy, and what is the role of the sluggish diffusion effect in this process?
item.material_system: TiCoCrFeMn high-entropy alloy (two-phase BCC solid solution + C14 Laves phase)
item.processing_route: Powder metallurgy: mechanical alloying of Ti, Co, Cr, Fe, Mn powders (5 h, argon) followed by sintering via U-FAST (modified Spark Plasma Sintering) at 1050 °C for 1 min, then homogenization annealing at 1000 °C for up to 1000 h in argon
item.test_conditions: Annealing times: 1, 10, 20, 50, 100, and 1000 h at 1000 °C in argon atmosphere; microhardness measured via Vickers method (0.025–1.0 kgf); grain size analyzed via EBSD; diffusion coefficients calculated from EDS linear scans
key_findings: Structural stability was achieved after 100 h of annealing, with stable grain sizes of approximately 2 µm for the BCC solid solution and 0.4 µm for the BCC+C14 mixture.
Long-term heating up to 1000 h caused grain growth to 2.7 µm (BCC) and 0.7 µm (BCC+C14), accompanied by a hardness decrease from 1065 HV to 1000 HV.
The highest grain growth rate was 0.0235 µm·h⁻¹ during the initial 10–50 h period due to non-monotonic chemical changes, while the two-phase region grew at 0.0081 µm·h⁻¹.
In the stable state (100–1000 h), grain growth slowed significantly to 0.0004–0.0007 µm·h⁻¹.
Diffusion coefficients stabilized at DCr = 1.28 × 10⁻¹⁹ m²·s⁻¹ and DTi = 1.04 × 10⁻¹⁹ m²·s⁻¹, demonstrating the sluggish diffusion effect.
The chromium diffusion coefficient in the alloy was three orders of magnitude lower than in the Ni3Al superstructure.
Non-monotonic changes in chemical composition between 10–100 h caused fluctuations in hardness and phase fractions before stabilization.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the high structural stability and slowed grain growth to the 'sluggish diffusion effect' and 'cocktail effect' typical of high-entropy alloys. The thermodynamically stable Laves C14 phase inhibits grain growth in the two-phase region, while the non-monotonic chemical composition changes during the initial 10–100 h drive phase reconstruction and mass transport, eventually leading to a stable matrix where the Hall-Petch relationship holds.
item.limitations: The text notes that the presence of coagulating titanium oxide precipitates (likely from unreduced powder surfaces and air compaction) prevented precise automated grain size analysis, requiring non-automated outlining. Additionally, in the ultra-fine two-phase regions, it was impossible to distinguish individual grains belonging to the solid solution versus the intermetallic phase, so they were analyzed as a common region.
item.future_work: The authors state that the detailed analysis of the hardness measurement models (H-K, PSR, MPSR, N-G) and their accuracy will be discussed in a separate work devoted only to this issue.
quotes: It was found that the tested alloy achieved structural stability after 100 h of annealing.
DCr = 1.28 × 10−19 (m2·s−1) and DTi = 1.04 × 10−19 (m2·s−1), demonstrating the sluggish diffusion effect typical of high-entropy alloys.
The observed 'seemingly inverse' Hall–Petch effect was not dependent on the grain size. In fact, it was primarily the result of momentary changes in the mechanical properties...
